title: What scaffold training does OSHA require for users and erectors?
description: What 29 CFR 1926.454 requires: qualified person training for scaffold users, competent person training for erectors and inspectors, and retraining triggers.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires construction employers, under 29 CFR 1926.454, to have every employee who works on a scaffold trained by a qualified person in the hazards of that scaffold type, and every employee who erects, dismantles, moves, operates, repairs, maintains or inspects a scaffold trained by a competent person. Retraining is required when worksite or scaffold changes, or inadequate performance, show an employee has lost proficiency.
keyTakeaways: 1926.454 sets two tiers: scaffold users trained by a qualified person under paragraph (a), and erectors, dismantlers, movers, operators, repairers, maintainers and inspectors trained by a competent person under paragraph (b).

User training must cover electrical, fall and falling object hazards, fall protection procedures, proper use and material handling, maximum intended load and load-carrying capacities, and other pertinent requirements.
Paragraph (c) requires retraining when site changes or scaffold changes introduce hazards the employee was not trained on, or when performance shows proficiency has been lost.
Unlike fall protection training under 1926.503, the scaffold standard does not prescribe a written certification record, so employers must decide what evidence to keep.
Scaffolding (1926.451) was fourth in federal OSHA's preliminary list of most cited standards for fiscal year 2026.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with OSHA-approved State Plans)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Construction employers whose employees perform work while on a scaffold
Employees who erect, disassemble, move, operate, repair, maintain or inspect scaffolds
Qualified persons and competent persons who train and supervise scaffold work
Trades using supported, suspended and mobile scaffolds, including masons, painters, plasterers and facade installers

blocks.text: Anyone who works on a scaffold, and, at a higher level, anyone who builds, changes or inspects one. [29 CFR 1926.454](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.454) is the training section of Subpart L, OSHA's scaffold standard for construction, and it separates the two groups by who must deliver their training.

blocks.caption: The two training tiers in 29 CFR 1926.454
head: Tier
Who it covers
Who must train them
Core content
rows: Paragraph (a): scaffold users
Each employee who performs work while on a scaffold
A person qualified in the subject matter
Recognize the hazards of the type of scaffold being used and understand procedures to control or minimize them
Paragraph (b): erectors and inspectors
Each employee involved in erecting, disassembling, moving, operating, repairing, maintaining or inspecting a scaffold
A competent person
Recognize hazards of the work in question, correct procedures for the specific scaffold, design criteria, maximum intended load and intended use

blocks.text: The distinction between a qualified and a competent person comes from OSHA's construction definitions in [29 CFR 1926.32](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.32). A qualified person has "a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing" or "extensive knowledge, training, and experience" and has demonstrated the ability to solve problems in the subject. A competent person can identify existing and predictable hazards "and who has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them."

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 29 CFR 1926.451 and 1926.454 and OSHA guidance as at November 2026. Fall protection outside scaffolds is covered by 1926.503, described on the [OSHA fall protection training](/regulations/osha-fall-protection-training-requirements) page. State Plan states may set different or additional scaffold rules.

sections.heading: What must scaffold user training cover?

blocks.text: It must cover five areas tied to the type of scaffold the employee uses. Paragraph (a) requires training "to recognize the hazards associated with the type of scaffold being used and to understand the procedures to control or minimize those hazards," including:

items: the nature of any electrical hazards, fall hazards and falling object hazards in the work area
the correct procedures for dealing with electrical hazards and for erecting, maintaining and disassembling the fall protection systems and falling object protection systems being used
the proper use of the scaffold, and the proper handling of materials on the scaffold
the maximum intended load and the load-carrying capacities of the scaffolds used
any other pertinent requirements of Subpart L

blocks.text: Because the training is tied to "the type of scaffold being used", training on a frame scaffold does not automatically cover a suspended or mobile scaffold. Fall protection is a central part of the content: [29 CFR 1926.451(g)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.451) requires each employee on a scaffold more than 10 feet (3.1 m) above a lower level to be protected from falling, which is a different threshold from the 6 feet used for most other construction surfaces.

sections.heading: What must erectors, dismantlers and inspectors be trained on?

blocks.text: They must be trained by a competent person on the hazards of the work and the correct procedures for the specific scaffold. Paragraph (b) lists the topics, "as applicable":

items: the correct procedures for erecting, disassembling, moving, operating, repairing, inspecting and maintaining the type of scaffold in question
the design criteria, maximum intended load-carrying capacity and intended use of the scaffold
any other pertinent requirements of Subpart L

blocks.text: Paragraph (b) covers more people than the job title "scaffold erector" suggests. An employee who moves a mobile scaffold, repairs a damaged plank, or performs the inspection is inside paragraph (b) and needs competent person training for that activity, not just user training.

When the employer has reason to believe an employee lacks the skill or understanding needed for safe scaffold work. Paragraph (c) requires the employer to "retrain each such employee so that the requisite proficiency is regained", and lists three situations where retraining is required, without limiting it to them:

items: changes at the worksite present a hazard about which the employee has not been trained
changes in the types of scaffolds, fall protection, falling object protection or other equipment present a hazard about which the employee has not been trained
inadequacies in the affected employee's work involving scaffolds indicate that the employee has not retained the requisite proficiency

blocks.text: There is no annual requirement. An employer that changes scaffold systems, adds suspended platforms or moves to a site with overhead power lines has a retraining event. A supervisor who observes overloading, missing guardrails or unsafe access should treat it as a retraining trigger and record it. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) for combining triggers with periodic refreshers.

sections.heading: What scaffold training records does OSHA require?

blocks.text: 1926.454 does not require a written certification or specify record contents. That differs from fall protection training, where 1926.503(b) prescribes a certification record. The employer still has to show that each user was trained by a qualified person and each erector or inspector by a competent person, on the type of scaffold in use, so in practice a record is the only way to prove compliance.

A useful record names the employee, the scaffold types covered, which tier (user or erector and inspector) the training satisfied, the trainer and the basis for their qualified or competent status, and the date. For retention approaches, see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How often are scaffold rules cited?

blocks.text: Frequently. OSHA's [preliminary top 10 cited standards](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) for fiscal year 2026 (October 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026) list Scaffolding, construction (29 CFR 1926.451) fourth across all industries. OSHA's [scaffolding overview](https://www.osha.gov/scaffolding) cites the Bureau of Labor Statistics Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries as reporting 52 fatal falls to lower levels from scaffolding in 2020. Many of the general requirements cited under 1926.451, such as guardrails, access and load limits, are topics that 1926.454 training must cover.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models scaffold types, roles and the two training tiers as a framework, then links each role and scaffold type to the specific hazards and procedures it must demonstrate. When a contractor adds a scaffold type, the framework shows which users and erectors need training before work starts.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require a scaffold training certificate?
faqs.a: No specific certificate is required by 1926.454. The standard requires training by a qualified person for users and by a competent person for erectors and inspectors. Employers commonly issue certificates or wallet cards, but the legal question is whether the training met paragraph (a) or (b) for the scaffold type in use.

faqs.q: How often does scaffold training need to be refreshed?
faqs.a: The standard sets no fixed interval. Retraining is required under paragraph (c) when worksite or equipment changes introduce hazards an employee was not trained on, or when performance shows proficiency has been lost. Employers may add a periodic refresher as policy.

faqs.q: Can the same person be both qualified and competent?
faqs.a: Yes. The definitions differ, but one person can meet both if they have the qualifications or demonstrated expertise of a qualified person and the hazard recognition and authority of a competent person. Employers should record the basis for each status, since paragraph (a) and (b) training require different trainers.

faqs.q: Do aerial lifts count as scaffolds for training purposes?
faqs.a: Aerial lifts are addressed in a separate section of Subpart L, 29 CFR 1926.453, rather than in the scaffold training section, so 1926.454 training does not cover them. Employers using both should treat them as separate training needs in their matrix.
